Ecopads work, but are they worth the trouble? - I have the Senseo SL7810 coffee maker, and to make the Ecopad fit I had to cut a plastic nub off the bottom of the filter. After that, it works as advertised, and it makes a decent cup of coffee. However, I'm not so sure it is worth the 25-30 cents per serving that you save by not buying prepackaged coffee pods. First you have to grind the coffee beans. Even pre-ground coffee is often too coarse and will need to be ground again. Then there is the messy job of transferring the finely ground coffee into the filter, a task that can seldom be accomplished without spilling some. Afterwards there is the messy cleanup where you need to use a lot of running water to clean grounds out of the filter. All in all, it's a time-consuming process. To me, the main purpose of getting a single serve coffee maker was as a time saver.

Very efficient!! - First of all I had my doubts that this would be as good as it is. I purchased this cooler to replace a 55Qt Lifetime cooler to avoid needing ice. I’m using it in an old pop up truck camper as a primary refrigerator/freezer.

When I first got it I thought it would be too small and didn’t like how there was a very large freezer side and the smaller side was the fridge. It didn’t appear the same internal size as my other cooler. After a week long trip I found the size was perfect and I could have taken more then I did. We also returned home with Frozen meals. When I camp I pre cook meals and vacuum seal them. They are then frozen I’m my house freezer and put in the cooler before the trip.

We hands down love this thing. It ran for two days on nothing but the deep cycle battery in the camper with no issues . It kept the frozen items frozen and the cold items cold and not frozen. I kept the settings on eco mode and the temp set for around 25-28F. The freezer side did freeze my OJ and made it a slushy only because I didn’t have room for it in the fridge side.

It should be noted that the cooler temp can only be set for the freezer side when the divider is in. It displays both temps on the screen though and with the above freezer settings usually hovered around the low 40’s in the fridge side.

The only complaint I have is the insulation value could be a little better especially in the lid however this can be easily fixed by putting a coat or blanket over the top (making sure not to cover the compressor vents).

All in all I would highly recommend this cooler!! For the price (cheaper then a lot of quality ice chests) it’s a great buy. I hope this helps anyone on the fence.

Do it right the first time and you won't have to fight with the dryer. - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!

Installation was easy but cramped (all the parts are under the door near the floor). but accessible. Hardest part was unscrewing the OLD 90 degree elbow off the old valve. If I had to do it again I would just get a new 90 degree elbow as it took 20 minutes and there are no good leverage points. Once I had everything teflon taped up again, installation is easy: screw in the supply line, replace the discharge hose and crimp, connect the plug to the solenoid, then single screw to hold it all in place. Has worked perfectly since, no leaks.
